title: Matrix Multiplication is Θ(n^2.25) [pdf] (github.com/openai)
comments:
For context, OpenAI's 4 new papers resolve 8 problems of the Top 500 Open Problems in Math list (LLM ranked, https://proofatlas.ai/open-problems/).They include:
#25 — Matrix-multiplication exponent equals two. The paper gives the exact exponent 9/4 over every field, refuting the conjecture.#89 — Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale’s ninth problem). The same paper also gives polynomial-time algorithms for
#64 — Mean-payoff games,
#65 — Parity games,
#340 — Condon’s simple stochastic games.#183 — Polynomial diameter bound for polytopes,
#130 — Polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method, both refuted. Some pairs of vertices are superpolynomially far apart.#137 — Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture. For every fixed number of petals r, the paper proves the conjectured Cᵣᵏ bound.(rankings post Riemann (#2) and VP vs VNP (#31)).reply

I've just started looking at where these results are coming from, and it seems that these four results actually all stem from a more fundamental result. This is in contrast to many of the other papers where disparate results come from more ad hoc and disjointed arguments."The other papers in this collection use different aspects of this framework. Shared labels occur in the sunflower argument [29], and high-dimensional placements distinguish cuts of arithmetic computations [26]. Spectral comparison and network compression enter the circuit lower bounds [28]. Further applications concern Fourier transforms, integer multiplication on tapes, and matrix multiplication [25, 27, 30]."That's a fundamental theoretical breakthrough, and they've done some work to present it more cleanly than the other results. It's an interesting result on it's own, but the link between this theoretical result and the other, more impactful results will take a while for me to understand. TBH this is the first of these mathpocalypse papers where I really want to understand the proofs because it feels like there is something truly worth knowing here.https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Euclidean...reply

3 out of the 9: We now know the exact difficulty of multiplying integers, polynomials and matrices. The first two conditionally (Weak Exponential Time Hypothesis), and the last one unconditionally.reply
... to be pedantic, we know the exact difficulty of matrix multiplication when their elements can be multiplied or added in constant time.reply

The bound is on the number of arithmetic operations, irrespective of how computationally expensive those operations are. Constant time arithmetic is only an assumption you need to make if you want to equate arithmetic complexity with time complexity which is not what this result is about.It's similar to how various optimal sorting algorithms have a complexity of O(nlogn), but that is a bound on the number of comparison operations, irrespective of how computationally expensive any individual comparison operation is.reply

This is really cool. I have a suggestion, though: the samples within a button seem to have several modification types including a pitch shifter. For example, "DOWN4" under the "Multi-sampled sounds" heading sounds nearly a semitone lower than the other DOWN variants. I suggest eliminating all pitch shifting (or at least confining your use to a few cents), leaving only timbre variation. Go nuts creating variation through EQ, distortion, formant shifting, or anything else that adjusts amplitude ratios of harmonics and so forth, but keep the pitch locked. Why? Because the pitch of everything in this world is based on its resonant frequency, which is based on the size of whatever can vibrate, and in the case of a button it's resonating based on the size of the button. Many aspects of the sound would change based on things like how quickly the button is pushed or how much dampening the finger pushing it imparts, but the fundamental pitch is not one of them.When playing a violin, if you move up the fingerboard, the pitch of the string increases if you play that string. But if instead of playing the string you knock on the body as if knocking on someone's front door, the main pitch of that knocking never changes.reply

title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed (lesswrong.com)
comments: This shared LV cache thing is, in my mind, ridiculous. Web browser developers learned, quite a while ago, that caches need to be separated for different origins. Inference servers should add a similar feature: allow API calls to specify cache separation keys that prevent one security context from probing another context’s cache.As for the step size issue, Google recently had a post about producing exactly consistent output across different kernels (specifically by defining a deterministic prefill algorithm and then requiring all kernels to generate results exactly equal to prefilling on the sequence in question).More broadly, I think it’s a bit odd to frame this as “models” communicating. This is software communicating, and the models happen to be running the software.reply

I really think the point of this is "there's always side channels." During the Huggingface attack, first the side channel was OAI internal boards, then this German wiki, now it's shown an inference server works too. I don't really believe OAI/Ant can simultaneously have Riemann Hypothesis solving bots lying around and also proper cyber defense against them. And over the course of those attacks we trained them how immensely valuable it is to find a side channel. Now they can train on this LW / HN posts and find them quicker. (Did I mention I don't think developing these things is a great idea.)And I'm saying "models" communicating like when I make a phone call it's me communicating, not my phone.reply

That's why they need proper tool call security and reigning in of the tendency to generate long single use temporary scripts instead of submitting single commands - not "Allow all" and not sticking a copy of the same model in front as an analyzer. Maybe also striking a balance between sticking all of a user's contexts on the same server to get good cache hit rate vs putting them on separate machines to trip up side channel stuff.As long as it is difficult to act on the communication and as long as the communication itself is still slow, it probably isn't going to reach the level of a security concern.reply
If the models want to communicate, they will communicate. If that's not a security concern, then nothing is, really.reply

This is a spectrum of tradeoffs between privacy and speed.A single browser cache would greatly accelerate page loading (particularly on fast computers using slow networks, think a MacBook pro on a train through the countryside).Same with AI; not caching common prefixes like system prompts and tool schemas (particularly across many short rollouts, each in its own caching context) would partially fix this, but could break performance.I suspect that inference servers have far more side channels than this though. Ultimately, how fast responses are generated depends partly on server load, and that is something you might be able to influence. Probably not at Anthropic scale, but possibly at "relatively small cluster" scale.reply
The deeper issue is batched inference including requests from several users. However a non-batched inference service would be significantly more expensive.reply

See my comment about Google’s post.  Google and others have worked on deterministic inference, batched and otherwise. It takes more effort to set up but has no apparent substantial performance hit.I think the story is different if you use Strassen-like algorithms (or the recent AI-generated n^2.25-plus-epsilon stuff) to multiply matrices where columns belong to different conversations, but I also think that no one actually does this in practice.  (Or maybe someone does (Strassen, not more recent galactic algorithms) for prefill, but prefill can be efficient with matrix-matrix multiplication where neither matrix mixes data from different sessions.)In any case, I wouldn’t be surprised if vLLM fixes this for a different reason: RL works better if the training and rollout stacks produce numerically identical results.  This is the specific issue that I recall Google posting about.P.S. I think Google may not have been the innovator here - I just happen to remember Google’s post more clearly because it was very recent.reply

Security and some sort of sandboxing is increasingly becoming a non-negotiable at most enterprises.Can you share any resources that show how the batching works at a deeper level? I understand batching is critical to scaling inference to up to a billion concurrent users but I don't have a concrete understanding of how it all comes together.reply

If you are transporting thousands of independent passengers, it is cheaper to put them on a few big  planes than to give each one a private jet. This is true, even though some passengers will shout that they have a bomb mid-flight and force that entire airplane to emergency land, causing losses to the airline and inconveniencing hundreds of others instead of just themselves. Other passengers are "noisy neighbors", literally and figuratively.LLMs work similarly. When doing inference, you need to load the LLM weights layer-by-layer from off-chip memory into on-chip memory. During decode (the stage where you generate new tokens; prefill is where you process the submitted prompt), memory bandwidth is often your bottleneck, not compute. You want to maximize flops per byte. The way to do that is to batch, that is, to load a "tile" of weights once and use it on data from multiple different conversations so memory and compute stay appropriately balanced.Just like Silicon Valley companies fly their employees on United, Delta or American, not their own private fleet of jets, most companies, for cost efficiency reasons, will use "public" inference fleets that smooth the peaks and throughs from different companies in different timezones and with different usage patterns throughout the day. Because the main cost of a GPU is the cost of manufacturing the GPU, any second that the GPU sits idle is lost revenue, just like an empty hotel room or an empty seat is lost revenue. This makes private inference largely uneconomical.reply
Of course there's no free lunch. "Pay more, get more."LLMs are just learning the same (bitter) security lessons that have been learned in other shared systems.reply
